correctness.rationale: For a rooted one-vertex union of k>=2 finite simple connected nontrivial graphs, inspected the root-suppressed deterministic nonroot closure. An eligible force persists until its target becomes blue, so the saturation is order independent. With initially blue root, nonroot branch states must all be A (self-completing) or exactly one B (needs one root force); at most one root force is possible. With initially white root, first saturate nonroot moves with root held white; completion additionally requires one branch activation alpha=1 to color the root. A/B branches with no activation are removed by barred polynomials. Thus Z(G;z)=(1+z)R((A_i),(B_i))-R((bar A_i),(bar B_i)), with R=prod A_i + sum_i B_i prod_{j!=i} A_j. Independently implemented ordinary global forcing and direct branch-state enumeration, exactly compared all coefficient dictionaries across 1,849 ordered 2-branch rooted assemblies of 43 connected labeled graphs of orders 2..4 plus 125 ordered 3-branch assemblies from 5 rooted graphs of orders 2..3: all 1,974 cases matched. The exact all-graph theorem rests on confluence and complete root-blue/root-white cases, not finite tests.
residual_risks: Requires a genuine articulation with disjoint connected branches meeting only at v.
No efficient polynomial-time computation from the four local polynomials is implied; defining them can be exponential.

value.rationale: An exact full coefficient polynomial at an arbitrary articulation is a significant motivated structural graph invariant theorem, answering a published explicit splitting-formula question. Four constructive rooted state polynomials count root-white activation and handle arbitrary cycles/blocks; it is substantially more informative than minimum forcing number and specialized bouquet formulas.
residual_risks: Constructive local subset enumeration need not be efficient; formula is separator-size-one only.

limitations: Finite simple connected graphs, root articulation with >=2 nontrivial connected branches, standard ordinary color-change rule.
